title: The Earnings Waterfall and the Cash Test

epigraph.quote: Our enterprise analytics software business did not generate positive cash flow from operations, and we do not expect it to generate sufficient cash flow from operations to satisfy our financial obligations or liquidity needs over the next twelve months.
epigraph.author: Strategy FY2025 Form 10-K

web_blocks.html: This is management’s own liquidity warning about the software business; it should sit beside, not beneath, any narrative about platform potential. [1]

web_blocks.title: Read the bridge in two passes

web_blocks.html: The deterministic FY2025 bridge below answers two different questions. First, what happened to the software revenue base before the digital-asset remeasurement? Revenue of $477.233 million less $149.417 million of cost of revenue produced $327.816 million of gross profit. Selling and marketing, research and development, and general and administrative expense summed to $368.725 million. That left a derived $40.909 million operating shortfall before the unrealized digital-asset loss. Second, what happened to reported operating income? The $5,403.476 million unrealized loss pushed the operating result to a $5,444.385 million loss. The reported components reconcile exactly in this FY2025-only waterfall. [1]

Those two passes must not be confused. The large asset remeasurement dominates the final reported operating-loss magnitude, but the pre-remeasurement shortfall is also real evidence: gross profit did not cover the disclosed selling, research, and administrative expenses. In ratio terms, the three listed expense categories totaled a derived 77.3% of revenue, while gross profit was a derived 68.7% of revenue; both percentages use FY2025 revenue of $477.233 million as denominator. The calculation is not a substitute for management’s own segment reporting, and the result before the fair-value loss is a reconstruction, not a separately reported non-GAAP measure. [1]

web_blocks.takeaway: The line-by-line table scales one audited fiscal year only. It separates the software cost base from the large non-cash digital-asset mark and reconciles the disclosed FY2025 operating result, net loss, CFO, and CFO-less-capex proxy. Employee costs and D&A are embedded in reported expense lines rather than separately disclosed in the supplied statement excerpt. [1][11]

web_blocks.title: Why a fair-value loss changes earnings without being customer economics

web_blocks.html: The filing’s digital-asset fair-value loss is an accounting remeasurement of an asset, not a software operating cost such as cloud hosting, customer support, or engineering payroll. Its scale can make the income statement a poor single-period proxy for the software operation. The reverse is equally important: removing the asset mark from your mental model does not make the operating business profitable by definition. The reported gross profit and the three listed expense categories still produce a negative subtotal before the remeasurement. You should keep a reported GAAP bridge and an explicitly labeled operating view side by side, never silently substitute one for the other. [1]

The company itself states that the enterprise analytics software business did not generate positive cash flow from operations in FY2025 and does not expect sufficient software cash flow to satisfy financial obligations or liquidity needs over the next twelve months. That disclosure is more direct than a generic risk factor: it addresses the cash-generating capacity of the software operation. The sanitized SEC facts extract also reports FY2025 operating cash flow of negative $67.241 million and capital expenditures of $8.212 million, for a derived operating-cash-flow-less-capex figure of negative $75.453 million. The separate extract is useful for the cash series, but it is not an input to the FY2025 income-statement waterfall. [1]

The FY2024 comparison shows why the FY2025 bridge should be read as an operating trend rather than a single isolated cost stack. Revenue increased from $463.456 million to $477.233 million, but gross profit declined from $333.988 million to $327.816 million as total cost of revenue rose from $129.468 million to $149.417 million. The corresponding gross margin is about 72.1% in FY2024 and 68.7% in FY2025, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue. This does not identify which customer, stream, or cost driver caused the change; the excerpt gives enough to see the direction, not to allocate the cause. [1]

web_blocks.title: Cash conversion is the harder operating test

web_blocks.html: A software business can report positive gross profit while consuming cash when operating costs, working-capital movements, and other operating cash items exceed cash collected after supplier and employee payments. In FY2025 the supplied company-facts series shows negative operating cash flow despite $477.233 million of revenue; in 2024 it was negative $53.032 million, and in 2023 it was positive $12.712 million. Those figures warn against treating recurring billing language as equivalent to cash conversion. The available facts do not provide a complete working-capital bridge by receivables, deferred revenue, payables, and accrued expenses, so you cannot assign the cash deficit to any one cause from this evidence alone. [1]

Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow was positive $14.267 million, compared with negative $45.612 million in the first nine months of 2025; nine-month capex was $3.181 million versus $7.628 million. This is a substantial year-over-year improvement in the supplied interim cash figures, but it does not erase the FY2025 disclosure or establish a durable annual cash profile. Nor should you combine those interim values with the FY2025 waterfall: the periods have different durations and the waterfall is intentionally one audited annual period. Continue to ask whether operating cash generation recurs across full fiscal years and whether it comes from customer operations rather than changes in financing or treasury activity. [2]

web_blocks.title: The counterweight: customer economics can improve, but proof remains incomplete

web_blocks.html: There are reasons not to reduce the software operation to its FY2025 loss. Cloud subscription revenue rose from $106.776 million in FY2024 to $175.657 million in FY2025, and Q3 2026 subscription revenue was $68.590 million compared with $45.972 million a year earlier. Q3 gross profit was $89.634 million on revenue of $125.427 million, a derived quarterly gross margin of 71.5%; the company’s release rounds this to 71%. The product is used in reported customer examples spanning pharmaceutical field analytics, insurance reporting, retail operations, and AI-assisted enterprise questions. These are positive signs of continued commercial activity, but they do not answer whether the recurring model ultimately covers sales, research, administration, and cash needs. [1][2][3][6][7][8][9]

The bear case is rooted in direct evidence rather than a hypothetical collapse. Subscription revenue is growing, but support and license revenue were lower in the Q3 comparison; full support for on-premises licenses ends on December 31, 2026. FY2025 operating expenses exceeded gross profit before the asset mark, and the company explicitly says software operations did not generate positive operating cash flow and will not meet the cited near-term liquidity needs. Customer stories give examples, not the retention, concentration, margin, or cohort data needed to validate a broad-based inflection. If you conclude that the product has value, you still have to ask whether the value is monetized with enough recurring gross profit and cash discipline. [1][2][6][7][8][9]

web_blocks.title: What the waterfall does not tell you

web_blocks.html: A single-period bridge is transparent, not complete. It traces FY2025 revenue through cost of revenue, the three disclosed operating-expense categories, the digital-asset mark, net interest and other non-operating items, tax benefit, net loss, and then a separate CFO-less-capex cash proxy. It does not allocate corporate spending among customers, calculate customer-acquisition payback, identify cloud cost by cohort, or split consolidated CFO into software and treasury operations. The right use is to orient questions and prevent the asset mark from hiding the software cost base—not to manufacture a normalized earnings claim. [1][11]

For a forward operating review, preserve the same separation every quarter: publish the GAAP result, identify the fair-value contribution, then show software revenue, gross profit, operating expenses, and cash conversion without implying that any one view replaces the other. The most informative trend would connect subscription growth to customer retention, stream-level gross profit, and cash collection. If subscriptions rise but support declines faster, or if gross profit expands while cash remains negative, the questions are different. The supplied materials do not provide enough cohort or segment cash data to run that complete test today, but they identify exactly which disclosures would make it possible. [1][2]

This distinction also protects you from false precision. A calculation such as CFO less capex is a useful cash proxy, but it does not explain timing effects or equal a fully reconciled free-cash-flow measure. A subtotal before the digital-asset loss is useful for isolating reported lines, but it is not an audited standalone software operating-income measure. Each derived figure should carry its formula and its boundary. When the company later supplies detailed working-capital and segment disclosures, you can refine the diagnosis; until then, it is more accurate to name the uncertainty than to transform a partial record into a definitive normalized result. [1][2]

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: You can say both things precisely: FY2025 reported operating loss was dominated by a $5.403 billion unrealized asset loss, and the software operation’s gross profit still fell short of the three disclosed operating-expense categories before that loss. A fair analysis refuses to let either clause disappear. [1]

book_paragraphs: A waterfall is valuable here because the income statement contains one line so large that it can distort every casual description of the year. Use FY2025 only, as the explicit period, and begin with the reported software revenue of $477.233 million. Deduct $149.417 million in total cost of revenue and you arrive at reported gross profit of $327.816 million. Then deduct $122.956 million of selling and marketing, $93.860 million of research and development, and $151.909 million of general and administrative expense. Those three expenses add to $368.725 million, leaving a derived loss of $40.909 million before the unrealized digital-asset loss. [1]

Next, include the reported $5,403.476 million unrealized loss on digital assets. The resulting arithmetic is a $5,444.385 million operating loss, which matches the reported FY2025 figure. The conversion from the filing’s USD-thousand presentation to USD millions is straightforward, and the bridge uses no interim or trailing figures. It continues below operating income using same-period FY2025 values for net interest expense, other non-operating expense, income-tax benefit, and net loss, then shows cash from operations and capex as a separate cash bridge. Employee costs and D&A are embedded in broader statement lines rather than separately disclosed in the supplied excerpt, and the CFO figure is consolidated rather than software-segment-only. [1][11]

This view gives you an important two-part conclusion. The accounting mark explains nearly all the magnitude of the reported operating loss; it is not a customer-delivery cost, and you should not use it as a measure of software unit economics. But the result before that mark is still negative. Gross profit was smaller than the sum of the three identified operating-expense categories. A reader who removes the fair-value loss and then calls the business profitable has skipped the remaining $40.909 million shortfall. A reader who points only to the $5.444 billion reported loss and calls the software product economically unviable has also skipped the distinction between remeasurement and operating activity. [1]

The annual cash-flow totals also show why consolidated liquidity should not be mistaken for software operating performance. The facts series lists FY2025 cash from investing of negative $22.512 billion and cash from financing of positive $24.844 billion, amounts much larger than annual software revenue. The supplied summary does not identify every transaction inside either total, so you should not attribute all investing outflow to one purchase category or treat financing inflows as customer cash generation. A complete liquidity review would reconcile the full statement and contractual obligations; the waterfall reconciles the income statement and then presents CFO less capex as a separate consolidated cash proxy; it does not reconcile the full investing and financing statement or isolate segment cash. [1]

The prior-year comparison keeps the discussion grounded. FY2024 revenue was $463.456 million, cost of revenue $129.468 million, and gross profit $333.988 million; FY2025 revenue rose to $477.233 million while cost of revenue reached $149.417 million and gross profit fell to $327.816 million. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives a derived gross margin of about 72.1% for FY2024 and 68.7% for FY2025. That compression is worth monitoring, but the provided excerpt does not allocate the cost increase by customer, product stream, cloud-hosting expense, or other driver. You can identify the observed change without claiming to know its cause. [1]

The proportions clarify the scale without pretending to produce a new accounting segment. Total operating expenses across selling and marketing, R&D, and G&A were 77.3% of FY2025 revenue, while gross profit was 68.7% of revenue; each percentage uses $477.233 million as denominator and is derived from the 10-K. The margin spread leaves little room for omitted expense categories or execution slippage. It also tells you where a business-quality argument must concentrate: either subscription growth and customer expansion eventually lift gross profit, operating expense growth is restrained, or both. The supplied sources do not establish that the necessary relationship has already been achieved. [1]

Now separate profit from cash. Strategy’s 10-K makes a direct statement that its enterprise analytics software business did not generate positive cash flow from operations in FY2025 and that it does not expect this business to generate enough operating cash flow to satisfy financial obligations or liquidity needs over the next twelve months. This is not an inference from the consolidated digital-asset loss; it is the company’s own description of software cash generation. The fundamentals extract reports company-wide FY2025 operating cash flow of negative $67.241 million and capex of $8.212 million. Subtracting capex yields a simple negative $75.453 million CFO-less-capex figure. It is a cash-flow proxy, not a complete free-cash-flow definition, and the filing’s software-specific statement should not be confused with a fully segmented cash-flow statement. [1]

Historical cash conversion reinforces the need for caution. The facts extract lists operating cash flow of positive $12.712 million in 2023, negative $53.032 million in 2024, and negative $67.241 million in 2025. Meanwhile, reported revenue was $496.261 million, $463.456 million, and $477.233 million respectively. Those three years show that revenue around the same broad scale did not consistently translate into positive operating cash. They do not, by themselves, reveal whether the swing came from customer collections, deferred revenue, employee compensation, supplier payments, taxes, or another operating item. The supplied extract lacks a detailed working-capital reconciliation, so any single-cause explanation would exceed the evidence. [1]

There is a more encouraging interim datapoint, but you should label its limits. In the first nine months of 2026, operating cash flow was positive $14.267 million and capex was $3.181 million, compared with negative $45.612 million and $7.628 million in the comparable 2025 period. On a like-duration basis, the change is favorable. It does not prove that the full year will be positive, that the cash is sourced only from a stable cloud subscription base, or that the next annual period will repeat it. Keep the interim comparison separate from the audited FY2025 income-statement waterfall and watch for cash generation to persist across full years. [2]

The income statement’s largest non-software line also changes the burden of proof for management’s operating narrative. If an asset remeasurement creates a multi-billion-dollar gain or loss, consolidated earnings can swing even when annual software revenue remains close to its prior-year level. That is why you should ask for operational measures alongside GAAP earnings: customer retention, cloud migration, gross profit by stream, and segment cash flow. Those measures would let a reader test customer economics directly. In their absence, the waterfall can only isolate the listed FY2025 expense structure and show where the reported result reconciles. [1][2]

The revenue mix contains a potential bridge toward better economics. Cloud subscriptions grew in FY2025 and in the Q3 2026 comparison; Q3 subscription revenue was $68.590 million versus $45.972 million a year earlier. Q3 gross profit was $89.634 million on $125.427 million revenue, or a derived margin of about 71.5%, consistent with the release’s rounded 71% figure. The cloud model typically has 36-month subscriptions, and the company is sunsetting support for on-premises licenses. Together, those facts support a hypothesis that recurring services could gain importance. But a hypothesis needs evidence of renewal, expansion, contribution margin, and collections—metrics not supplied in the permitted record. [1][2][3]

Customer stories add color without closing the cash question. The vendor’s examples describe Pfizer’s distributed user community, Helsana’s report consolidation, B&H Photo’s retail analytics and cloud migration, and Lotte’s governed AI agents. They suggest that the platform can be embedded in workflows where consistent information matters. They do not publish contract margins, deployment cost, renewal rates, customer-level revenue, or independently verified payback. A successful project may strengthen retention and support revenue, but you cannot calculate those effects from the stories. Treat them as evidence of product use cases and reported customer outcomes, not as substitutes for audited cash conversion. [6][7][8][9]

You should also distinguish the waterfall’s arithmetic from a claim about cash-generating power. The unrealized digital-asset loss appears in operating income in the reported FY2025 bridge and is removed only when you describe the derived subtotal before that line. Nothing in that subtraction changes cash collected from customers, costs paid to employees, or the timing of working capital. Conversely, cash flow includes noncash adjustments and balance movements that do not appear as a simple revenue-minus-expense calculation. The two statements answer different questions, and a strong operating analysis reconciles both instead of selecting whichever result best fits a prior view. [1]

The bear case does not require predicting product failure. It is enough to observe that in FY2025 the listed operating-expense categories exceeded gross profit, company management said software operating cash flow was insufficient for stated near-term needs, and legacy-license support is ending on a fixed timetable. The bull case is also testable: cloud subscriptions are growing, customers describe valuable deployments, and the first nine months of 2026 showed improved cash flow against the prior period. The hinge between them is whether recurring software gross profit and cash generation can scale while the legacy mix contracts. That question belongs to operations and accounting, not to the asset’s mark-to-market volatility. [1][2][6][7][8][9]

Finally, respect what the bridge cannot say. It does not produce a normalized earnings estimate, a full enterprise-software standalone statement, or a forecast. It does not allocate selling, research, or administrative costs to individual revenue streams. It does not calculate a cash return on customer acquisition. It does not tell you how much of a consolidated cash movement reflects treasury purchases or financing. By stopping at the supported line and showing the arithmetic, you preserve the difference between reported fact, derived subtotal, and unresolved question. That discipline is more useful than a polished but unsupported adjusted result. [1][2]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The disciplined conclusion is not that the accounting mark is irrelevant; it is that it answers a different question. Show the mark, then show the software cost base that remains after you isolate it. [1]

book_callouts.title: EVIDENCE BOUNDARY
book_callouts.text: The FY2025 waterfall uses single-period audited P&L inputs, SEC company-facts below-the-line and cash-flow inputs, and separately labels reported versus derived lines. [1][11]
